product: القَهْوَة/الشَّاي في قالب ثلج منحوت — Coffee (and now matcha/tea lattes) poured into a hollowed, hand-carved block of crystal-clear ice; drunk through a straw, then the inner wall — which has turned to coffee sherbet — is eaten with a spoon. Japanese: 氷の器のアイスコーヒー ("ice-vessel iced coffee") / 氷の器のコールドブリュー. Two canonical originals: 北野坂にしむら珈琲店 (Kitanozaka Nishimura Coffee, Kobe) and cafe 33 at Hyatt Regency Kyoto.
origin:
INVENTOR AND DATE — the English-language internet gets this wrong by about fifty years. Tasting Table and Boing Boing say the drink "began in 2022"; Japankuru says "as early as 2016" (that 2016 date is only the earliest big web write-up, GIGAZINE, 24 Aug 2016). The Japanese record is unambiguous.

It was invented at 北野坂にしむら珈琲店 (Kitanozaka Nishimura Coffee Shop), Yamamoto-dori 2-1-20, Chuo-ku, Kobe, around 1973, by the shop's owner. The trigger is documented: he was served a dish on a plate made of ice at a washoku (Japanese-cuisine) restaurant and adapted the idea to coffee (ITmedia ねとらぼ interview with the shop, 25 Aug 2022; Excite News). The first vessels were carved by hand with chisels (鑿).

The parent company, 神戸にしむら珈琲店 (Kobe Nishimura Coffee), was founded in 1948 in the port city of Kobe by 川瀬喜代子 (Kawase Kiyoko), starting with three tables (official company story page, kobe-nishimura.jp; ja.wikipedia — note the official site credits Kawase Kiyoko while some accounts name 西村善三郎). In 1974 the founder converted the ground floor of her own home into 北野坂にしむら珈琲店 — 日本初の会員制喫茶店, Japan's first members-only coffee house, furnished with imported antiques and furniture she carved herself. The ice-vessel coffee was born inside that members-only room; it was a private amenity for members, not a public menu item. The shop's own official X account states it plainly: 「1974年から長きにわたりご愛顧いただいている夏季限定メニューです」 — "a summer-only menu item cherished since 1974" (@nishimura_cs, 1 July 2024). The Kitanozaka store was only opened to the general public after the 1995 Great Hanshin-Awaji earthquake — which is why a 50-year-old drink felt "new" to the world in 2022.

Constraints that have never changed: July and August only; Kitanozaka branch only (not at any of the other Nishimura stores); no reservations, no holding ("ご予約やお取り置きはいたしておりません"); first come, first served.

THE SECOND ORIGIN — THE LUXURY NODE. cafe 33, on the ground floor of Hyatt Regency Kyoto (644-2 Sanjusangendo-mawari, Higashiyama-ku), launched 氷の器のコールドブリュー on 1 July 2022, running to mid-September, ¥1,800 incl. tax and service, five per day, 14:30–17:00, reservation required. The coffee is cold brew from 小川珈琲 (Ogawa Coffee, a Kyoto house), water-extracted with no heat. The vessel is custom-ordered, frozen over 72 hours, and hand-carved one by one by a veteran Kyoto ice craftsman from local groundwater, so no two are identical (Hyatt Regency Kyoto PR Times releases; Japanmiru). This is the version that actually went global, because it is inside an international hotel that tourists photograph.

Nishimura is the inventor. cafe 33 is the exporter.
virality:
This did not go viral once. It went viral four separate times, each bigger, and each time you can name the account and the date.

WAVE 0 — TELEVISION, c.2012. The shop itself told ITmedia: 「10年ぐらい前にテレビで紹介されたときには通年の3倍ぐらいの反響がありました」 — a TV feature about ten years before 2022 produced roughly three times the normal year's response. (ITmedia ねとらぼ, 25 Aug 2022.)

WAVE 1 — INSTAGRAM, c.2019. Same interview, same shop, direct quote: 「3年ほど前のInstagramでの紹介からは爆発的に人気が出ており」 — from an Instagram feature around 2019, popularity became explosive. This is the moment a 45-year-old members-only curiosity became a queue. The shop also notes that from around 2021, other companies began offering the same thing in growing numbers ("昨年あたりから他社でも同じような提供をされているところが随分と増えてきています") — the copycat wave is dated by the originator itself.

WAVE 2 — THE TWEET, AUGUST 2022. YouTuber いきなり若旦那 (@wakadanna_coo) posted a photo captioned 「神戸でアイスコーヒー頼んだらアイスの中にコーヒー入ってるヤツきた……」 ("I ordered an iced coffee in Kobe and got the one with the coffee inside the ice…"). It spread, and the Japanese press followed within days: ITmedia ねとらぼ ran the shop interview on 25 Aug 2022; the Kobe Shimbun ran it in September 2022 under the headline 「今年も爆発的ヒット」 — "another explosive hit this year." The business detail in that Kobe Shimbun piece is the useful part: despite ¥2,000 a cup and a 20–30 minute wait from order to serve, on some days it sold out within two hours of the 10:00 opening.

WAVE 3 — JUNE 2023, THE INTERNATIONAL IGNITION. This is the moment the brief asks about, and it is a cluster, not a single post. NextShark credits the traveling video to Instagram user @jukananan727 (じゅかな, "Japan Food Trip", ~1M followers on Instagram; HypeAuditor lists 1.2M), posted June 2023, filmed at cafe 33. In the same week three TikToks landed — decoded from their video IDs: @foodwtf on 7 June 2023, @humotti on 9 June 2023 (captioned 氷の彫刻グラスで飲む絶品アイスコーヒー, listing the cold brew at ¥2,000, 完全予約制), and @jesseogn on 11 June 2023 — "When I ordered an ice coffee in Kyoto, and ended up with coffee inside of ice…" — which carries 67.8K likes and 141 comments; @jesseogn has 1.6M TikTok followers and 83.6M total likes. He posted the same reel to Instagram the same day (11 June 2023).

Then Kobe's own summer caught it, July–August 2023: @humotti 1 July 2023 (¥2,000, captioned "the painfully cold block-ice coffee you melt clear with the heat of your hands"), @muni_gurume_japan 3 July, @saya___0805 24 July, @japan.explore 3 Aug, @goodlife Instagram reel 11 Aug, and on 21 August 2023 @franklinthewoman posted to both TikTok and Instagram within sixteen minutes of each other — that TikTok stands at 587.3K views and 30.6K likes; her account has 493.5K TikTok followers and 22.3M lifetime likes. A YouTube Short, "The coolest iced coffee in Japan," went up the same day, 21 Aug 2023.

WAVE 4 — MARCH–SEPTEMBER 2024, THE REPOST ECONOMY AND WESTERN PRESS. Aggregator accounts re-cut the @jukananan727 footage: @coffeeders on 4 March 2024 and @coffeeholic101 on 26 March 2024, both crediting her. One such repost — Republic World attributes it to the account "The Coffee Lifestyle" — reached 3.1 million views and 93,000 likes, and produced the line that became the drink's slogan in the comments: "That's not iced coffee. That's coffeed ice." Western coverage followed in sequence: NextShark, 13 May 2024, syndicated onward to Yahoo Lifestyle; Tasting Table, 27 July 2024; Boing Boing, 21 September 2024; plus Japankuru, HYPER JAPAN, grape Japan and Gigazine. Kobe's 2024 summer produced its own posts — @dsebaji 2 July 2024, @franklinthewoman again 11 July 2024, now quoting ¥2,300.

WHAT IT DID TO THE BUSINESS — the price is the cleanest proof. At Nishimura: ¥2,000 (2022–23) → ¥2,300 (2024) → ¥2,500 incl. tax for the 1 July–31 Aug 2025 season, still selling out. At cafe 33 the escalation is violent: ¥1,800 at launch in 2022 → ¥2,000 in 2023–24 → ¥3,300 a cup in 2025/26, ¥4,200 with cake — and the Japanese trade headline is 「1杯3300円でも予約殺到！？氷の器で味わう幻のコーヒー」 ("Reservations flooding in even at ¥3,300 a cup — the phantom coffee served in an ice vessel"), which also notes the short videos of it running to 数百万再生, several million plays. Supply stayed capped at 5–10 servings a day. Demand was so far ahead of supply that the drink is literally nicknamed 幻 — "phantom."

The franchise then extended into TEA, which matters for a cold-drinks brand: Hyatt Regency Kyoto launched 氷の器 series #2, an iced matcha latte in the same ice vessel, on 5 August 2025 (matcha from a long-established Kyoto tea house, whisked to order, poured over lightly sweetened milk for a green/white layered effect), and series #3, an iced strawberry latte, on 1 April 2026 at ¥5,500 for the set with strawberry-cube croissant and ice cream.

CAVEAT ON HASHTAG TOTALS: TikTok removed public hashtag view counts in February 2024 (Washington Post, 8 Feb 2024), so no current live total exists for #にしむら珈琲, #氷の器のアイスコーヒー or #iceblockcoffee. The surviving category-level aggregates are TikTok #icedcoffee at 17.2 billion views (a pre-Feb-2024 hashtag aggregate, not a single video) and #icecoffee at 267.6K posts.

hard_to_copy:
Six structural moats, in order of how hard they are to buy your way past.

1. PHYSICS, NOT RECIPE — THERMAL SHOCK. You cannot pour coffee into a vessel taken straight from the freezer; the temperature differential cracks it. Nishimura tempers every vessel, which is why service takes 15–20 minutes per cup before the coffee even arrives, and 20–30 minutes from order to table. That is an un-compressible constraint. Any competitor who tries to make this fast destroys the product on the pass, in front of the customer.

2. THE VESSEL IS A 72-HOUR ASSET. cafe 33's blocks are custom-ordered and frozen for 72 hours before carving. That means your inventory is committed three days before the customer walks in, and unsold inventory is not stock — it is a puddle. Nobody can flex this to demand.

3. CLARITY IS A CAPITAL PROBLEM. Crystal-clear ice requires directional freezing. The industry-standard machine, a Clinebell CB-300, runs roughly $3,800–$7,000 (used units around $4,500) and yields only two 300 lb blocks (20" × 40" × 10") per three-day cycle. Cloudy ice reads as cheap on camera and kills the entire proposition. So the barrier is: buy the machine, wait three days, and still only get two blocks.

4. IT IS HAND CARVING, AND HAND CARVING DOESN'T SCALE. Nishimura buys block ice from an ice supplier it has worked with for decades, then its own staff carve each ~15 cm cube vessel individually. cafe 33 uses a veteran Kyoto ice craftsman and local groundwater; no two vessels are identical. The consequence is a hard supply ceiling — 5 to 10 servings a day at cafe 33 — and that ceiling is what created the ¥3,300 price and the 幻 ("phantom") nickname. Scarcity here is not marketing; it is arithmetic.

5. AN OUTSIDER'S COST OF ENTRY IS DOCUMENTED. Et-Si café in Hyderabad — one of the few confirmed copiers — spent two to three months in R&D purely on the structure, thickness and clarity of the block so it would hold a beverage for ~45 minutes without collapsing, and prices the result at ₹595. That is the real entry cost for a competitor who already knows exactly what the answer looks like.

6. THE ORGANISATIONAL MOAT NOBODY TALKS ABOUT. Nishimura Coffee runs all of its ~11 stores directly, refuses to franchise, has deliberately confined itself to Kobe and the Hanshin corridor rather than going national, and does not let an employee brew coffee for customers until they have trained for at least three years. You can copy the ice. You cannot copy a fifty-year-old members-only room in Kobe, or a staff that carves ice as part of a craft ladder.

AND THE REASON IT LOOPS ON CAMERA — WHICH IS ITSELF A MOAT. The product changes state during consumption. It arrives frosted and opaque; the drinker warms it with their hands (uncomfortably, memorably cold) and the surface goes clear; by the end the coffee appears to float inside transparent glass; and the inner wall touching the coffee has turned to a coffee-flavoured sherbet that is scraped out with a spoon. Every other viral drink is one photograph. This one is a three-act video with a payoff, which is precisely why creators keep re-shooting it across four years instead of one season.

WHITE SPACE FOR SHABIM: In the Arab world this exists only in the UAE — The Pods on Bluewaters Island, Dubai serves a "Signature Ice Cube Coffee" (latte, cappuccino, matcha latte, rose latte, affogato) from around AED 125, promoted by Time Out Dubai on 16 July 2024 and again 7 May 2025 and featured by Curly Tales on 14 Sept 2025; and La Letizia Café & Shisha in Dubai Marina does a giant ice-cube mug. Repeated searching in Arabic and English surfaced NO ice-vessel coffee operator in Saudi Arabia (Riyadh/Jeddah — the viral drink there is the chocolate-shell "cracked" mocha), Kuwait, or Iraq. Baghdad and the Saudi market are open ground, and Dubai proves Gulf customers will pay roughly AED 125 (~$34) for it.
